claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Component authors can change a component's internal design and include the state migration in the same release.
Pulumi's component state migrations are a new feature.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migration feedback exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.

Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block that can be shared across projects and teams, and users work with inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
A modern AWSX VPC component exists that users can upgrade to from the legacy AWSX VPC component.
The pulumi/examples repository contains an AWSX VPC state migration example at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with v1, v2, and v3 versions.
The legacy component is exposed as `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc`.
In the example's v1, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading from the legacy to the modern AWSX component could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
Because a security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC means replacing the AWS security group too (per the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId property documentation).
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data.
The example does not create a database.
The example's v2 upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The example's v3 removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example's v1, Pulumi tracks awsx:x:ec2:Vpc as the top-level component with children aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet (containing Subnet, RouteTable, RouteTableAssociation) and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway (containing aws InternetGateway); in v2 tracks awsx:ec2:Vpc with aws Vpc as child and Subnet/RouteTable/RouteTableAssociation and InternetGateway beneath the VPC; in v3 tracks aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc at the top.
Pulumi's state records both the physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components.
Modern AWSX removes the subnet and internet gateway wrapper components and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In this example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
Aliases alone cannot remove component wrappers and transfer references to the replacement resources; a state migration is needed to describe that whole change together.
To migrate to modern AWSX, the new VPC component is registered with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option.
`migrateClassicVpc` comes from the example's v2/migration.ts file in pulumi/examples at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration.
The alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the state migration callback receives the old component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A Pulumi state migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records that replace the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
The example migration callback is safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, it does nothing.
The example migration callback raises an error on an unexpected component type instead of guessing how to migrate it.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.
The two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.

Pulumi uses successor mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, so a security group outside the VPC component keeps its reference to the migrated VPC record with the same AWS VPC ID.
The example's v3 declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.

The second migration (v3/migration.ts in the example) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record; the VPC keeps its AWS ID and the other resources remain beneath it.
The v3 VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX) and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means users can skip versions without having to edit stack state by hand.
After a state migration, Pulumi compares the new program with the migrated state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
The example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags after migration, even though resource IDs are kept.
The example should be run starting with v1 following its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
Before each upgrade in the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and the update (`pulumi up`) saves the migrated state.

When a component registers its migration inside its implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update when they upgrade the component.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without changes.
The component state migrations guide at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covers the callback contract.
The VPC example in pulumi/examples contains all three programs and the migration code shown in the post.
Pulumi docs pages exist at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ and /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) must be idempotent.
A Pulumi state migration callback must return no result when the resource state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
The option reference for the `stateMigrations` resource option, including its callback API, is at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api.
Component state migration callback state entries use the Pulumi checkpoint resource format, which includes fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached to a component when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results from component state migrations (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
